card.name: Lurish dances
card.tagline: Vibrant scarf circles and martial stick duels of the Iranian plateau.
card.profile: Lurish dances encompass a broad range of traditional folk forms originating among the Lur communities of Western and Southwestern Iran. Performed in colorful attire during celebrations, weddings, and communal gatherings, these styles range from mixed-gender circle dances (Čupi) waving bright handkerchiefs to martial wood-striking duels (Čubâzi). The mass circle dances traditionally follow an accelerating structural continuum that moves from the deliberate Sangin-Samâ into the dynamic Sepâ and culminates in the explosive Dopâ tempo. Rich archeological records—including first-millennium BC bronze flags and ancient petroglyphs—trace the roots of these movements deep into the antiquity of the Iranian plateau.
card.insight: Artifacts from Tepe Giyan and petroglyphs at Kul-e Farah establish that Lurish collective circle dancing predates the Aryan migrations to the Iranian plateau.
card.profile_long:
### Origins and History
Lurish dances are deeply rooted in the historical landscape of the Iranian plateau. Archeological excavations in Lurish-inhabited areas—such as Kozagaran, Tepe Giyan, Tepe Musiyan, CheghaMish, and Kul-e Farah—reveal motifs depicting dancing figures and musicians on ancient pottery and petroglyphs. Bronze flags from Luristan dated to the first millennium BC portray dancing figures, providing concrete evidence that the lineage of Lurish dance predates the historic Aryan migrations into the region. Over generations, these ancient movement traditions evolved alongside the everyday agricultural life, martial history, and social structures of Lur groups, including the Feylis, Bakhtiari, and Southern Lurs.

### How It Is Danced
Movement within Lurish traditions is broadly categorized into mass circular dances (Čupi), handkerchief dances (Dasmâl-bâzi), and martial dueling (Čubâzi). In the Čupi mass circle dance, men and women link hands or intertwine pinky fingers, relying shoulder-to-shoulder under the guidance of a lead dancer known as the Sarčupi or Čupikeš. The circular sequence unfolds in phases: it begins with Sangin-Samâ, where dancers step their right foot across the left in a cross, take two steps forward, touch the tip of the left toe to the ground, and draw it beside the right foot with arms bent at the elbow. As the music speeds up, the line transitions into Sepâ (three steps), stepping forward on the right foot and flexing the knees rhythmically. The acceleration peaks in Dopâ (two steps), a fast and vibrant phase, before eventually reversing back to Sangin-Samâ. In Dasmâl-bâzi, dancers wave bright scarves held in each hand. In contrast, Čubâzi features a dramatic martial duet: one dancer wields a heavy four- to five-foot stick to defend below the knees, while an attacker attempts to strike with a flexible twig (tarka); the defender escapes solely by leaping high into the air.

### Music and Instruments
Lurish dances are closely tied to regional musical ensembles. The Čupi mass dances and Čubâzi stick fights are driven by powerful outdoor acoustic instruments, primarily the sorna, karnâ horn, and heavy drums (tombak or dohol), alongside the fiddle and strike instruments often referenced as tochmal music. The musical phrasing provides clear cues for the dancers: a slow, steady pulse dictates the initial Sangin-Samâ, gradually building speed through the drum patterns to signal the switch to Sepâ, and reaching high-velocity cadences during Dopâ.

### Costume and Setting
Visual vibrancy is central to Lurish dance, defined by bright, colorful traditional clothing worn by both men and women. Dasmâl-bâzi dancers carry bright, fluttering scarves (dastmâl) in each hand, creating fluid visual waves that amplify hand movements across the circle. Čubâzi and Čupi are typically performed outdoors or in open village spaces, where audience members form large cheering rings around the performers.

### Occasions and Meaning
Lurish dances serve both festive and ritual functions within community life. Mass circle dances and Dasmâl-bâzi are focal points of weddings and festive celebrations. Čubâzi is performed as a celebratory martial display, frequently serving as an exciting prelude to Bakhtiari wedding ceremonies. Specific functional dances also mark agricultural moments, such as harvesting ceremony dances, while solemn mourning dances like Chamariuna are performed among Feylis, Bakhtiaris, and Southern Lurs upon the death of loved ones.

### Regional Variants and Lineage
Dasmâl-bâzi is particularly prevalent among the Southern Lurs and Bakhtiari people. The martial stick dance Čubâzi (or Tarka-bâzi) is also strongly maintained within Bakhtiari and Southern Lur communities. Mourning dances like Chamariuna highlight distinct regional expressions among Feyli Lurs and Great Lur tribes, underscoring a continuous lineage of shared movement across diverse Lur geography.
card.sacred_note: While not inherently sacred, specific forms such as Chamariuna are solemn mourning rituals performed for deceased loved ones and should be approached with cultural reverence.

sections.origins_and_history: Archeological excavations in Lurish-inhabited areas—including Kozagaran, Tepe Giyan, Tepe Musiyan, CheghaMish, and Kul-e Farah—demonstrate that Lurish dance predates Aryan migrations into the Iranian plateau. Pottery motifs depicting three dancing figures and bronze flags from Luristan dating to the first millennium BC provide physical evidence of ancient dance traditions. Musicians and instruments depicted on petroglyphs in Kul-e Farah and CheghaMish further confirm the antiquity of dance across these regions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Lurish dances include circular group styles (Čupi), scarf dances (Dasmâl-bâzi), and martial stick duels (Čubâzi). In Čupi, dancers join hands or fingers shoulder-to-shoulder, guided by a lead dancer called the Sarčupi (or Čupikeš). The circle moves through distinct phases: Sangin-Samâ begins slowly with a cross-step of the right foot over the left, two forward steps, a toe-tap of the left foot, and arms bent at the elbow; Sepâ accelerates the movement into three forward steps starting on the right foot with knee flexes; Dopâ pushes the tempo to its fastest point before reversing back. In Dasmâl-bâzi, dancers wave colorful scarves (dastmâl) held in each hand. In Čubâzi, two dancers compete: an attacker wielding a short flexible stick (tarka) targets the opponent below the knee, while a defender holding a long stick (four to five feet long) must leap into the air to avoid the strike.
sections.music_and_instruments: Lurish dance relies heavily on traditional wind and percussion instruments, such as the karnâ horn, drums, strike instruments, and fiddles (often referred to as tochmal music). The drum and horn accompaniment regulates the progressive speed of Čupi dances, accelerating from the slow tempo of Sangin-Samâ into the rapid beat of Dopâ.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear brightly colored folk garments. In scarf dances, men and women carry vibrant handkerchiefs (dastmâl) in both hands. Performances typically take place in outdoor open-air spaces or during community celebrations, surrounded by rings of spectating audiences.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dances are performed for life-cycle events, seasonal work, and ritual commemorations. Čupi and scarf dances feature prominently at weddings and festive gatherings. Čubâzi serves as a celebratory martial spectacle, often presented as a prelude to weddings. Other specialized forms include harvesting ceremony dances, PaPoshtePa dances, Suwaruna, and solemn mourning dances such as Chamariuna performed for deceased loved ones among Feylis and Southern Lur tribes.
sections.regional_variants: Dasmâl-bâzi and Čubâzi are widely practiced among the Bakhtiari and Southern Lur communities. Mourning dances such as Chamariuna are specific to Feylis and Great Lur tribes (including Bakhtiaris and Southern Lurs).
sections.lineage: Lurish dances represent an unbroken tradition passed down through generations across Lur-inhabited regions, with iconographic roots traceable to first-millennium BC Luristan bronzes and prehistoric Iranian plateau petroglyphs.

basic_steps: Cross the right foot over the left foot.
Touch the tip of the left toe to the ground.
Bring the left foot beside the right foot.
Transition into three forward steps starting with the right foot (Sepâ phase).
teaching.rhythm: Progressive acceleration starting with a slow steady tempo (Sangin-Samâ), speeding up to a medium three-step meter (Sepâ), and reaching a fast peak (Dopâ).
teaching.formation: Closed or open circular ring (Čupi) shoulder-to-shoulder, or paired duet arrangement (Čubâzi).
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with the foot placement and cross-steps of Sangin-Samâ before trying faster tempo shifts.

claims.text: Luri dances include a range of folk dances popular among different groups of Iran's Lurs.

Motifs depicting three dancing persons appear on pottery and bronze flags of Luristan from the first millennium BC.
The mass dance starts with Sangin-Samâ, accelerates to Sepâ, reaches Dopâ, and returns to Sangin-Samâ.
In Čubâzi stick dance, the attacker holds a tarka stick while the defender holds a long heavy stick up to four or five feet long.
The lead performer in Čupi mass dance is called Sarčupi or Čupikeš.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Slow steady pulse accelerating into rapid driving drum strikes.
music_profile.vocal_style: Audience cheering, screaming, and whistling accompanying instrumental music.
music_profile.musical_form: Sectional acceleration continuum transitioning from Sangin-Samâ to Sepâ, Dopâ, and returning to Sangin-Samâ.
music_profile.sound_description: A driving combination of resonant outdoor horn calls (karnâ), melodic fiddle lines, and heavy drum strikes that steadily build in speed to propel circle dancers.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, shoulder-to-shoulder contact in circular lines with elbows bent.
movement_profile.footwork: Right foot crosses left, two steps forward, left toe touch to side, stepping forward right-left-right with knee flexion.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Pinky fingers linked at shoulder height, or waving colorful scarves held in both hands.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Controlled torso following directional step movements.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Circular chain lead by a Sarčupi, moving counter-clockwise or in place; or paired central dueling space.
movement_profile.partnering: Linked hands/fingers in mass circle; attacker and defender pairs in Čubâzi.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Gradual buildup from deliberate, heavy stepping to high-energy rapid footwork.

signature_moves.name: Sangin-Samâ step
signature_moves.description: Cross right foot over left, step forward twice, touch left toe to ground, and align feet.

signature_moves.name: Sepâ step
signature_moves.description: Three forward steps starting on the right foot followed by knee flexion.

signature_moves.name: Čubâzi leap
signature_moves.description: High vertical jump performed by a defender to dodge a stick strike aimed below the knees.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Grounded footwork in Čupi mass dances; high vertical explosive leaps in Čubâzi.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid breaking the locked hand-holding line in Čupi; in Čubâzi, strikes must never target above the knee.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the arm bends and hand/scarf waving movements while seated in a chair, executing simplified forward toe taps.
seniors.standing_version: Perform Sangin-Samâ slow steps while holding a secure handrail or partner's hand, avoiding rapid speed shifts.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Maintain a slow, constant tempo without accelerating into Dopâ; restrict footwork to small steps.

children.game_version: Play a leader-follower game led by a designated 'Sarčupi' who changes scarf movement patterns on drum cues.
children.counts: Count 1-2-3 forward steps with exaggerated knee bends.
avoid: Using solid wooden sticks for martial sparring
